pages.x: Paraguay, a small country deep inland on the rivers of South America, had been closed off for decades by strong rulers and had built one of the biggest armies on the continent. In 1864, when Brazil sent troops into Uruguay to back one side in a civil war there, Paraguay's leader Francisco Solano López went to war with Brazil.

When Argentina would not let his army cross its land to reach Brazil, López invaded Argentina too. In May 1865 Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, now under a friendly government, signed the Treaty of the Triple Alliance and swore to fight on until López was gone. Together they had more than twenty times as many people as Paraguay.

In May 1866 the allies invaded Paraguay and threw back a huge Paraguayan attack at Tuyutí, the biggest battle ever fought in South America. Then they were stuck for two years in the swamps before the river fortress of Humaitá, losing men to cholera and to bloody failed assaults.

Brazil bore most of the fighting. Its emperor, Pedro II, a scholarly man who loved science, refused any peace while López ruled, and Brazil freed many enslaved men to fight in its armies. In January 1869 the allies took Asunción, Paraguay's capital, and Brazilian troops occupied it.

López fought on in the hills with an army of old men and boys. At Acosta Ñu in August 1869 thousands of children, some with beards painted on to look older, fought Brazilian troops, and Paraguay still keeps its Children's Day on that date. By the end, women far outnumbered men, and it was women who rebuilt the country.

pages.x: On 1 March 1870 Brazilian cavalry caught López at Cerro Corá in the northern hills. Refusing to surrender, he was killed beside a stream, crying out, it is said, that he died with his country. Paraguay lost land to Brazil and Argentina and stayed occupied for six years.

Eliza Lynch, an Irish woman López had met in Paris, ruled Paraguay's society at his side and followed his army to the end; she buried him and their son, it is said, with her own hands. Blamed for decades for the disaster, she is honoured in Paraguay today as a heroine.

It was the deadliest war in the history of South America. Paraguay, once one of the continent's most self-reliant states, was left in ruins and took generations to recover. In Brazil the war made the army powerful, and helped bring the end of slavery in 1888 and of the empire in 1889.
